symptoms: Water-soaked or blister-like spots on leaves
Green or yellow lesions that can turn dark
Leaves may progressively dry and decompose
early_signs: Initial watery-looking spots on foliage
Lesions developing under cool and humid conditions
favorable_conditions: Fog, drizzling and dew accumulation on leaves
notes: BAMIS also lists chemical control recommendations. They are intentionally excluded from this initial entry pending separate label and registration verification.

symptoms: Small oval gray or white lesions on leaves
Dark brown margins around lesions
Lesions may enlarge and become eye-shaped
Severe infection can cause leaves to appear scorched
early_signs: Small gray or whitish spots on rice leaves
Dark brown borders around initial lesions
low_cost_actions: Maintain appropriate water in the field
favorable_conditions: Cool nights and warm daytime conditions
notes: Management recommendations are summarized from the official AIS rice disease guidance.

symptoms: Circular brown spots on older lower leaves
Concentric target-like rings within lesions
Multiple lesions may merge and damage leaf tissue
Affected leaves may turn yellow and fall
early_signs: Small circular brown spots on older lower leaves
low_cost_actions: Remove and destroy infected crop residues
Control weeds and alternative host plants
favorable_conditions: Rain splash and wind can spread infection
notes: Symptoms and cultural management summarized from AIS. Chemical recommendations intentionally omitted.

symptoms: Water-soaked irregular patches on leaves
Patches become dark brown or black
White fungal-like growth may appear on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Infection may spread to stems and fruits
early_signs: Pale green water-soaked patches on leaves
low_cost_actions: Avoid unnecessary irrigation during disease development
favorable_conditions: Cloudy humid weather and light rain
notes: Symptoms and environmental conditions summarized from AIS. Chemical recommendations omitted.

symptoms: Leaves and stems wilt rapidly
Plant may die without obvious leaf spots
Discoloration may occur inside the lower stem
Bacterial streaming may be visible when infected stem sections are placed in water
early_signs: Partial wilting of leaves or branches
Wilting may progress rapidly
notes: AIS describes bacterial wilt symptoms, transmission and cultural management.

symptoms: Leaves curl and become distorted
Plants become stunted
Leaves may become thick and brittle
Fruit production may decrease
early_signs: Upward or inward curling of young leaves
Abnormal leaf growth
low_cost_actions: Keep the field free of weeds that can host vectors
notes: AIS describes leaf curling, stunting and whitefly-mediated transmission.

symptoms: Brown circular spots on older leaves
Concentric rings inside lesions
Multiple spots may merge into larger damaged areas
Affected leaves may dry and curl
early_signs: Small brown circular spots on older leaves
low_cost_actions: Remove infected crop residues after harvest
favorable_conditions: Rain splash and wind can spread infection
notes: AIS discusses early blight affecting potato and tomato. Full source review is pending.

symptoms: Partial wilting of leaves or branches
Wilting can progress rapidly
Plant may die prematurely
Bacterial streaming may be visible from a cut stem placed in clear water
early_signs: One leaf or branch begins to wilt
Partial wilting may occur before the whole plant collapses
low_cost_actions: Avoid moving contaminated soil or irrigation water between fields
Stop irrigation in affected areas and seek local agricultural advice
notes: AIS discusses bacterial wilt affecting potato, brinjal and tomato. Full source review is pending.
BAMIS provides favorable weather information for potato scab, but this entry deliberately leaves symptoms and management empty pending further source verification.

symptoms: Small sesame-seed-like spots initially appear on leaves
Spots enlarge with pale or whitish centers and brown margins
Multiple spots may merge and damage leaf tissue
Infected grains may become discolored and poorly developed
early_signs: Tiny brown spots on rice leaves
Small spots gradually enlarge and develop pale centers
low_cost_actions: Maintain balanced nitrogen and potassium fertilizer
Maintain appropriate water management in the field
favorable_conditions: Cool nights and warm daytime conditions
Light sandy soil with low water-holding capacity
notes: Symptoms, disease cause and cultural management summarized from the official AIS rice disease publication. Chemical recommendations are omitted pending separate label and registration verification.

symptoms: Bluish water-soaked lesions initially appear near leaf tips or edges
Lesions gradually turn yellow
Infection progresses downward along leaf margins
Severely affected leaves become dry and straw-colored
Young seedlings may wilt and die in severe infections
early_signs: Small bluish water-soaked areas near leaf tips
Yellow discoloration developing along leaf margins
low_cost_actions: Avoid injuries to roots and plants during transplanting
Apply urea in appropriate split doses
Avoid additional urea top-dressing after disease symptoms appear
Remove and destroy infected crop residues after harvest
notes: Symptoms, causal organism, favorable conditions and cultural management summarized from the AIS bacterial blight section. Chemical recommendations omitted.

symptoms: Water-soaked green lesions appear on the leaf sheath near the water level
Lesions develop gray centers and brown margins
Lesions may merge and spread to upper leaf sheaths and leaves
Severe infection can make patches of the field appear scorched
early_signs: Small water-soaked green spots on the lower leaf sheath
Gray centers and brown margins begin developing around lesions
low_cost_actions: Use disease-tolerant rice varieties where available
Maintain recommended spacing between transplanted seedlings
Remove and destroy infected crop residues after harvest
notes: Symptoms, causal organism, favorable conditions and cultural management summarized from the official AIS rice disease publication. Chemical recommendations omitted.

symptoms: Irregular grayish-brown lesions develop on the uppermost leaf sheath
Lesions have gray centers and brown or reddish-brown margins
Lesions may enlarge and merge across the sheath
Young panicles may remain trapped inside the sheath or emerge partially
Rotting may occur inside the sheath with whitish fungal growth
Affected grains may become discolored and poorly filled
early_signs: Small irregular brown lesions on the upper leaf sheath
Discoloration around the sheath enclosing the young panicle
low_cost_actions: Manage insect pests that can injure leaf sheaths
Remove infected crop residues after harvest
source_name: AIS Bangladesh, BAMIS/DAE and Bangladesh Rice Journal
notes: Symptoms and cultural management summarized from ACI Crop Care's Bangladesh rice disease reference. Causal organism cross-checked against Bangladesh Rice Journal. Favorable weather and booting-stage information cross-checked against BAMIS/DAE. Chemical recommendations omitted.

symptoms: Affected plants develop wilting
Wilting can progress to the whole plant
Severely affected plants may die
early_signs: Wilting begins in an affected plant
low_cost_actions: Use resistant varieties such as BARI Begun-8
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops such as rice, wheat or maize
Manage irrigation carefully in infected fields
Avoid planting brinjal repeatedly in contaminated soil
source_name: Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) and Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE)
notes: BARI Technology #58 documents integrated management of brinjal bacterial wilt. DAE Bangladesh Pest Risk Analysis identifies Ralstonia solanacearum as the causal organism. Detailed symptom descriptions and environmental thresholds require further verification.

symptoms: Small pale or grayish sunken spots develop on fruits
Spots have brownish halos
Lesions enlarge and develop concentric rings
Infected fruits become soft and watery
Severe infection can cause fruits to turn black and mummified
Circular gray to brown spots may also develop on leaves
early_signs: Small pale sunken spots on fruits
Grayish spots with brownish halos
Small circular gray or brown leaf spots
low_cost_actions: Collect and destroy infected fruits and crop debris
Avoid repeatedly growing brinjal in the same field
Monitor plants regularly for early symptoms
favorable_conditions: Infected crop debris in the field
source_name: Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University, Department of Plant Pathology
notes: Symptoms, causal organism, seed-borne nature and environmental observations summarized from the 2015 M.S. research thesis on Phomopsis fruit rot of eggplant. Cultural hygiene actions are included; chemical recommendations omitted.

symptoms: Leaves become unusually small and malformed
Young leaves develop tiny chlorotic structures
Flower buds become upright instead of pendulous
Flowers may become leaf-like structures
Short branches and small leaves create a bushy rosette appearance
Infected plants may produce no fruits or hard, tough fruits
early_signs: Reduction in the size of newly developing leaves
Abnormally shaped young leaves
Shortening of branches and internodes
low_cost_actions: Use yellow sticky sheets as part of integrated vector management
source_name: Bangladesh Biosafety Portal and Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute
notes: Symptoms and phytoplasma association summarized from the Biology of Brinjal reference. BARI Annual Report 2019-20 records a trial in which yellow sticky polythene sheets significantly reduced disease severity in 2019; results were not consistent across all trial years.

symptoms: Older leaves may bend downward and wilt
Yellowing may begin on one side of the plant
Brown discoloration may occur in stems and roots
Wilting can gradually spread throughout the plant
Severely affected plants may die
early_signs: Yellowing and wilting of older leaves
Wilting may initially affect one branch or side of the plant
low_cost_actions: Avoid planting in contaminated soil where possible
notes: Causal organism and symptoms summarized from AIS tomato disease guidance. Cultural management is summarized from its recommendations. Chemical recommendations omitted.

symptoms: Small brown water-soaked circular spots develop on leaves
Lesions may have yellowish halos
Older leaves may develop extensive spotting and defoliation
Green fruits may develop raised water-soaked spots
Fruit lesions may become rough and slightly sunken
early_signs: Small water-soaked brown spots on leaves
Yellowish halos surrounding leaf lesions
low_cost_actions: Monitor leaves and green fruits for early symptoms
source_name: Biology of Solanum lycopersicum, Bangladesh Biosafety Portal
notes: Symptoms, pathogen association and favorable weather summarized from the tomato biology reference. Exact current taxonomy should be checked before publication.

symptoms: Light and dark green mottling appears on leaves
Young leaves may wilt during sunny conditions
Leaflets become distorted, puckered and smaller
Fern-like leaf symptoms may occur
Affected plants may become stunted and pale green
early_signs: Irregular light and dark green mosaic patterns
Distortion and puckering of young leaves
low_cost_actions: Clean and disinfect tools used on plants
Avoid touching healthy plants immediately after handling infected plants
Monitor plants for abnormal leaf mottling
favorable_conditions: Contaminated hands, clothing and agricultural implements
source_name: Biology of Solanum lycopersicum, Bangladesh Biosafety Portal
notes: Symptoms and contact transmission summarized from the tomato biology reference. The source describes TMV; do not assume all tomato mosaic symptoms have this exact viral cause.

symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots develop on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to brown velvety growth appears underneath leaves
Spots may merge into larger affected areas
Leaves gradually yellow, dry and fall
Severe infection can cause extensive defoliation
early_signs: Small pale yellow patches on upper leaf surfaces
Early olive-green growth on the lower leaf surface
notes: Symptoms and management summarized from University of Minnesota Extension. This is an international reference, and its environmental guidance should be validated for Bangladeshi field conditions.
